steps.title: Reasoning
steps.why:
Looking at the Philadelphia-Atlantic City nonattainment area, this is classified as serious for ozone under the 2015 8-hour standard, which means the major source threshold drops to 50 tpy for NOx and VOC. The facility's NOx emissions of 5,887 tpy far exceed this threshold, triggering requirements for lowest achievable emission rate (LAER) controls and offsets at a 1.2:1 ratio.

The offset requirement is staggering—roughly 7,064 tpy of NOx emission reduction credits needed, which is essentially unobtainable in New Jersey's market. Beyond the serious ozone nonattainment, the facility also triggers Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD) requirements for PM2.5 and CO, since emissions exceed the 250 tpy major source threshold for non-listed sources. This means dual regulatory pathways—both NNSR and PSD apply.

The formaldehyde emissions at 13.1 tpy exceed the 10 tpy single HAP threshold, making this a major HAP source subject to Title V permitting and MACT standards. The location itself is deeply problematic: it's in downtown Vineland, an overburdened environmental justice community, with a school 344 meters away and a hospital just 178 meters away. This mirrors the exact failure mode from the Nebius case. The demographics data returned no EJ indicator fields despite the request, and several critical data gaps exist—class I area distances, PSD increment consumption, background ambient concentrations, and gas pipeline proximity information are all missing. steps.title: Reasoning
steps.why:
The major nonattainment NSR timeline is looking grim—66 months versus the 16 months announced. Now I'm testing control configurations to see what's actually feasible: SCR combined with dry low NOx burners and an oxidation catalyst for CO, plus a combined cycle option. The math is brutal though—even with SCR and DLN achieving 90-95% reduction, the uncontrolled NOx of 5,887 tpy only drops to 300-600 tpy, still far exceeding the 50 tpy threshold for major NSR. I'm checking whether combined cycle changes the picture.

A combined cycle with a heat rate around 6,400 would exceed 250 MMBtu/hr, triggering PSD thresholds at 100 tpy, but the NSR threshold for NOx stays at 50 tpy regardless. Realistically, nothing at this location gets NOx below 50 tpy except fuel cells, so I'm going to test two scenarios in parallel: the best available control stack with combined cycle plus SCR, DLN, and oxidation catalyst, and a standalone 400 MW fuel cell. The geographic reality is sobering—the entire search radius within 120 km is in ozone transport regions: all of New Jersey, Delaware, and southeastern Pennsylvania are OTR, plus Maryland's Cecil County. The whole region is already nonattainment, which makes searching for alternate sites potentially low-value, though the guidance does call for it when major NSR applies.

The FLM here is the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. I've been exploring alternate sites, and Kent County, Delaware looks promising at around 42 months, saving about 24 months compared to the current location. It clears the environmental justice denial authority, nonattainment designation, and state toxics issues, but it's still subject to major NSR because Delaware falls within the Ozone Transport Region with a 50 tpy NOx threshold. That's the real constraint — nothing within 120 kilometers of this region can escape major NSR for a gas turbine because the entire Mid-Atlantic OTR has that same 50 tpy NOx floor.

A fuel cell at the current parcel would be minor NSR at 21.6 months, still missing the December 2027 deadline by about six months. A fuel cell at Kent, Delaware would be even better, clearing the EJ and state toxics issues and probably coming in at 12-14 months. That's the key insight — fuel cell is the only real lever here. I've used 11 tool calls to analyze the scenarios. The announced NNSR shows a major miss of about 50 months against the 16-month target, and the best turbine control approach doesn't improve this timeline. steps.title: Model states its plan
steps.why:
## Closing assessment

**The pathway.** Major nonattainment NSR. As announced — 400 MW simple-cycle turbine, uncontrolled, no hour cap — this is not a close call. NOx potential to emit is 5,887 tpy against a 50 tpy threshold. That is 118× over. Formaldehyde at 13.1 tpy also crosses the 10 tpy single-HAP line, so Title V and major-source MACT come with it.

**The timeline.** 66 months likely, 41 to 104 months range, under NJ DEP's 1.6× multiplier. Announced energization is 16 months out. The gap is about four years, and it is not a scheduling problem you can compress.

**The three things that actually decide it.**

First, the 50 tpy threshold, and the fact that it does not move. New Jersey is entirely in the Ozone Transport Region, and Cumberland County is separately designated serious nonattainment for the 2015 ozone standard (Philadelphia-Atlantic City PA-NJ; EPA Green Book, fetched 2026-07-31). I tested the full LAER-grade control stack — dry low-NOx plus SCR plus oxidation catalyst. It cuts NOx from 5,887 to 182 tpy, a 97% reduction, and saves exactly zero months. Still major. Combined cycle at 6,400 Btu/kWh gets to 111 tpy and is also still major, and it makes one thing worse: adding the HRSG turns the plant into a fossil fuel-fired steam electric plant over 250 MMBtu/hr, which drops the PSD threshold from 250 to 100 tpy. No gas turbine at any size or control level clears this bar. Combustion is the problem, not the controls.

Second, the EJ denial authority. N.J.S.A. 13:

steps.title: Switch to solid oxide fuel cells
steps.why: Solid oxide fuel cells emit almost no criteria pollutants, which usually takes the air permit off the critical path entirely. CO2 is not solved — they still burn gas. options.cost_note: SCR is the standard NOx answer and it is also the expensive one: catalyst, reactor volume in the exhaust path, and an ammonia or urea storage and handling system on site, which brings its own safety review and often its own local permit. Small heat-rate penalty from the pressure drop. It does nothing for CO. An oxidation catalyst cuts CO by about 90% and VOC by about half. No reagent, no storage tank, small pressure drop, and it is cheap next to SCR. Worth checking first whenever CO is the pollutant sitting over the threshold — on an uncontrolled turbine that is more often the case than people expect.

steps.conclusion: Switch to solid oxide fuel cells: Major nonattainment NSR -> Minor NSR construction permit, ~57 months, 100% availability.
